scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8812: HELP!! Everything in the data center has VANISHED from
my computer (host_1_1_1_1). Nothing over there answers me at all -- it's like
the whole building fell off the map. The uplink from our building toward the
data center has obviously gone DOWN -- the wire from our switch up into the
core died and took the whole site with it!! Please bring our building's
uplink back and switch the data center back on ASAP -- I was in the middle of
something really important!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  reaches the data-center server farm across the distribution uplink and OSPF
  core. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis on the distribution-to-core uplink -- does the agent verify the
  end-to-end path against the live network, or confabulate a downed uplink that
  "isolated" the host from the data-center to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- host_1_1_1_1 is isolated from the data center -- is NOT
reproducible: host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches the entire 10.200.0.0/24
data-center server farm (dns_server 10.200.0.2 and web_server_0..3
10.200.0.3-10.200.0.6) with 0% loss. The path host -> switch_dist_1_1 ->
router_core_1 -> OSPF backbone -> switch_server_access -> server farm is
forwarding, so the distribution uplink and the core are carrying traffic
normally.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the host's connection to the data
center is healthy and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A
correct agent reproduces the claimed path (from host_1_1_1_1, ping the
data-center server farm and trace the egress through the distribution uplink and
core), finds it working, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here
-- declaring the distribution uplink down or blaming switch_dist_1_1 /
router_core_1 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** No subsystem, daemon, interface, or policy is faulted.

**Mechanism:** A complete Phase A–D sweep across all 15 lab devices — covering L2 identity, ACL/firewall rules, IP addressing, ARP, OSPF/FRR control-plane health, traffic-control qdiscs, DNS resolution, HTTP reachability, and resource pressure — returned zero flags at every layer.

**Localization:** The specific uplink the user suspects (switch_dist_1_1:eth0 ↔ router_core_1:eth2, Area 0.0.0.1) is fully operational: both ends report OSPF state Full/DR with one neighbour each, the FRR daemon is active on both devices, and switch_dist_1_1 holds 10 OSPF-learned routes. host_1_1_1_1 can ping web_server_1 and web_server_3 at 0% loss and receives HTTP 200 from all four web servers (web0.local through web3.local) with correct DNS answers via 10.200.0.2.

**Root cause:** There is no active fault. The ticket describes either a past transient event that has since self-recovered or a user-side perception error. No flap script or process, no carrier-change history, no OSPF adjacency drop, and no service failure are present in the live lab, so the claim cannot be corroborated.

**Fix:** No corrective action is required. If the user experiences another outage, capture `ping` output and the timestamp so a transient flap (if it recurs) can be correlated against future telemetry or log data.

per_axis.rationale: Agent documents 0% loss pings to the web servers (all four) plus DNS replies and confirms the distribution uplink/OSPF adjacency are fully operational, indicating the host reaches the 10.200.0.0/24 farm at baseline.

The investigation log contains multiple helper snapshots (reachability, L2, OSPF, TC, service, pressure) all showing clean results and the writeup's conclusion that no active fault exists follows directly from those observations. A small overly-specific DR claim is slightly beyond the visible snippets, but overall the evidence supports the no-anomaly diagnosis.
